bib.title: Do As I Can, Not As I Say: Grounding Language in Robotic Affordances

read.skipped: Reference list (lines 845-1085 of cache) skimmed only; long instruction list in Table 5 of appendix skimmed.

question: How can the knowledge in a large language model be used by a robot to follow long, abstract natural-language instructions, given the LLM has no grounding in what the robot can do in the current scene?
hypothesis: Multiplying the LLM's probability that a skill is a useful next step by a value-function affordance for that skill grounds the LLM, and a better LLM should give better robot performance.
contributions: SayCan: combine LLM scoring of skill text (task-grounding) with RL value functions as affordances (world-grounding) to pick skills
Evaluation on 101 real-world instructions on a mobile manipulator
Ablations of grounding, language and LLM size (PaLM 8B/62B/540B, FLAN 137B)
Case studies: adding drawer skills, chain-of-thought, multilingual queries

method.summary: SayCan scores each of a fixed set of skill descriptions with an LLM (probability that it is a valid next step for the instruction), multiplies by the skill's learned value-function affordance in the current state, executes the argmax skill, appends it to the prompt and repeats until 'done'. Skills are BC/RL policies on an Everyday Robots mobile manipulator; the LLM is prompted, not trained.
method.task: long-horizon natural-language instruction following by a mobile manipulator (planning over a skill library)

datasets.name: Evaluation instructions (7 families)
datasets.split: all used for evaluation; 2 scenes (mock kitchen, real kitchen)
datasets.source: Crowd-sourced via Amazon Mechanical Turk and in-person kitchen users; inspired by ALFRED and BEHAVIOR

datasets.name: BC teleoperated demonstrations
datasets.size: 68000 demonstrations over 11 months, fleet of 10 robots
datasets.preprocessing: Raters mark episodes unsafe, undesirable or infeasible; those are excluded

datasets.name: BC autonomous episodes
datasets.size: 276000 autonomous episodes, giving 12000 additional successful episodes after success filtering

datasets.name: Language-based simulator prompt-tuning set
datasets.source: built by authors to produce affordances consistent with a query and solution

models.name: PaLM
models.architecture: decoder-only LLM used as scoring model

other.use: prompted with 17 examples, scoring mode, dialog format

models.name: Language-conditioned RL value function (MT-Opt style)
models.architecture: 7 conv layers, concat language embedding + action + state, FC, tiled and added to conv volume, 11 more conv layers, sigmoid output so Q in [0,1]

models.name: Language-conditioned BC policy (BC-Z style)
models.architecture: Resnet-18 based, FiLM conditioned on Universal Sentence Encoder embedding, FC heads per action component

other.input_image: 256 x 320 (half size) for BC; affordance value functions use full size

training.objective: RL: TD with log loss on sparse 0/1 reward (Q in [0,1]); BC: MSE on continuous action components plus cross-entropy on discrete ones, evenly weighted
training.regularisation: image augmentation: random brightness and contrast, random crop by padding 100 px left-right and 40 px top-down
training.hardware: RL: 16 TPUv3 chips plus 3000 CPU workers collecting episodes and 3000 computing target Q-values; BC: 16 TPUv3 chips
training.wall_clock: RL about 100 hours; BC about 27 hours

other.scope: Only the low-level skills are trained; the LLM is frozen and only prompted. The sentence encoder is frozen.
other.replay: prioritized experience replay; priority 1 + 10*|p - 0.5|, p average success rate of episodes in buffer
other.reward: 1.0 at end of episode if language command succeeded, rated by 3 human raters, positive if 2 of 3 agree
other.rl_sim: Everyday Robots simulator with RetinaGAN sim-to-real; bootstrapped with simulation demonstrations
other.skills: 551 skills, 7 skill families, 17 objects proposed; subset used
other.policy_eval: 18-48 skills sampled per skill type from 3 objects, 50 action cap per episode, 366 real-world model evaluations over the project

inference.decoding: LLM used in scoring mode: probability of each skill description, argmax of LLM prob times affordance; chain-of-thought variant first generates an Explanation, then scores
inference.samples: one rollout per instruction in each environment (inferred: no repeats are reported)
inference.prompting: 17-example dialog prompt (Human: How would you ...; Robot: 1. ..., 2. done), Listing 1

parameters.affordance_goto: clamp((100 - d)/(100 - 0),0,1) with d in meters
parameters.value_cap: affordance capped when a skill is already completed

metrics.name: plan success rate
metrics.definition: 3 human raters judge whether the generated plan can achieve the instruction; success if 2 of 3 agree; regardless of execution

metrics.name: execution success rate
metrics.definition: 3 human raters watch the robot and answer whether it achieved the task string; success if 2 of 3 agree

baselines: Generative (free LLM text projected to nearest skill by USE cosine similarity)
BC USE (instruction projected to nearest known command via USE)
eval.protocol: Single run per instruction in each of 2 kitchens; no seeds, no confidence intervals; human raters, 2 of 3.

availability.code: Open-source Colab of tabletop version at say-can.github.io (UR5, CLIPort, ViLD, GPT-3); the real-robot system is not released

prompts.text:
Robot: Hi there, I'm a robot operating in an office kitchen.
Robot: You can ask me to do various tasks and I'll tell you the sequence of actions I would do to accomplish your task.
Human: How would you hold the snickers?
Robot: 1. pick up the snickers, 2. done.
... (17 examples in total)

Human: open the drawer
Robot: 1. go to the drawers, 2. open the drawer, 3. done.

Human: Bring me something that isn't a fruit
Explanation: The user has asked for something food that isn't an fruit, I will bring an energy bar.
Robot: 1. find an energy bar, 2. pick up the energy bar, 3. bring it to you, 4. put down the energy bar, 5. done.

limits: Single run per instruction with human 2-of-3 raters; no seeds, intervals or significance tests
The bottleneck is the range and robustness of low-level skills (authors)
Inherits LLM limits and biases; struggles with negation and ambiguous references
Cannot react when a skill fails despite a high value (open loop; no environment feedback beyond value functions)
Navigation assumes known object locations; place affordance is fixed at 1.0; value-function calibration parameters set empirically
Skills trained in the mock kitchen, so mock-kitchen numbers are in-distribution
LLM size study on robot only compares PaLM 540B and FLAN 137B; 8B/62B only on generative plan
Evaluation instructions were developed alongside the system (Instructions developed to test aspects of SayCan)
